1.note: Asaph is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of anguish over the invasion of Israel. If your language has a comparable way to express this feeling, you could use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [O God, nations have invaded your inheritance]

Here Asaph is introducing the **nations** as new participants in the psalm. He does not specify which nations, but refers to foreign peoples in general. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [foreign nations]

Here Asaph is speaking of the land of Israel being different than other parts of the earth by calling it God’s **inheritance**. This means the land that God specially reserved for him and his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into your special possession]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into what you have inherited]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who are holy]

1.q: בָּ֤אוּ גוֹיִ֨ם ׀ בְּֽ⁠נַחֲלָתֶ֗⁠ךָ טִ֭מְּאוּ אֶת־הֵיכַ֣ל קָדְשֶׁ֑⁠ךָ שָׂ֖מוּ אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֣ם לְ⁠עִיִּֽים
1.note: These three phrases all describe the enemy’s attack on what belongs to God. Each phrase intensifies the devastation, moving from invasion to defilement to destruction. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on how to translate parallel phrases see the Psalm 79 Introduction. Alternate translation: [nations have invaded your land, made your holy temple unclean, and turned Jerusalem into piles of rubble]

2.note: Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **bird** that lives in **the heavens**, that is, the sky. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the birds that fly in the sky]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they have given the flesh of your faithful as food to the beast of the earth]

Asaph is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean people who are faithful to God. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your faithful ones]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **beast** that lives on **the earth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the animals that live on the land]

The terms **the bird** and **the beast** are singular collective nouns that refer to all birds and all beasts as a group. If your language does not use singular nouns in that way, you can use plural forms in your translation.

Asaph is referring to all wild creatures by naming two major components, **bird of the heavens** and **beast of the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to every kind of bird … to every kind of wild creature]

3.note: Here, **their blood** represents their violent death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the blood of those they killed]

The point of this comparison is that just as **water** flows freely and abundantly, so the blood of the slain was shed in great quantity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as freely as water is poured out]
Asaph is providing background information to help readers understand the situation. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

4.note: Here Asaph is using the word **We** to introduce the community of Israel as speakers for the first time in the psalm. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [We, your people, have become]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The poetry of the original language was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [those whom our neighbors insult and mock]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people whom others reproach]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and we have become scorn and derision to the ones around us]

The terms **scorn** and **derision** mean similar things. Asaph is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [utter mockery]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **scorn** and **derision**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [people whom others scorn and deride]

5.q: עַד־מָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה תֶּאֱנַ֣ף לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח תִּבְעַ֥ר כְּמוֹ־אֵ֝֗שׁ קִנְאָתֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: These two phrases **Will you be angry forever** and **Will your jealousy burn like fire** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. The poetry of the original language was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [How long, Yahweh, will you remain fiercely angry with us]

Asaph is using the question form to express lament and anguish rather than to seek information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, it has been so long!]

Asaph is using the question form to express anguish at the duration of God’s anger rather than to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Please do not stay angry forever!]
Asaph says **forever** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [without end]

Asaph is using the question form to express distress rather than to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not let your jealousy keep burning like fire!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **jealousy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how jealous you are cause us to]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fire** is intense and consuming, so is God’s jealousy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as intensely as a fire burns]

6.q: שְׁפֹ֤ךְ חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֨ אֶֽל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֮ אֲשֶׁ֪ר לֹא־יְדָ֫ע֥וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠עַ֥ל מַמְלָכ֑וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ֝⁠שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֗ לֹ֣א קָרָֽאוּ
6.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request to God rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please.” For more information on imperatives, see the Psalm 79 Introduction. See how you as a team have decided to translate imperatives and follow that approach here and throughout this Psalm. Alternate translation: [Please pour out your wrath on the nations that have not known you and on the kingdoms that have not called on your name]

Here Asaph is speaking as if God’s wrath were a liquid that he could **pour out**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Unleash your wrath]

6.q: שְׁפֹ֤ךְ חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֨ אֶֽל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֮ אֲשֶׁ֪ר לֹא־יְדָ֫ע֥וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠עַ֥ל מַמְלָכ֑וֹת
6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Show the peoples that do not worship you how angry you are and also the kingdoms]

6.q: וְ⁠עַ֥ל מַמְלָכ֑וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ֝⁠שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֗ לֹ֣א קָרָֽאוּ
6.note: Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and pour out your wrath on the kingdoms that have not called on your name]
Here, **name** represents who God is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you]

7.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here Asaph is speaking as if the enemy were a wild animal that **devoured** its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one has destroyed the people of Jacob]
The pronoun **one** is indefinite and refers to the enemy nations mentioned in verse 6. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the enemy has devoured]

Asaph is using the name **Jacob** to represent the nation of Israel, which descended from the patriarch Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Israel]
The pronoun **they** shifts from the singular “one” and refers to the enemy nations. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the nations have desolated]
The pronoun **his** refers to Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s habitation]

8.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked things we did in the past]

Asaph is speaking of **your compassions** as if they were a living thing that could **meet** the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [show us compassion]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [come to us with your tender care]

Asaph is giving the reason for his urgent request. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this gives the reason for the preceding request. Alternate translation: [because we have become very weak]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God, the one who saves us]

Here, **on account of the glory of your name** marks the purpose for the preceding request. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that your name will be glorified]
Here, **name** represents God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your glorious reputation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your glorious name]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sins**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wrong things we have done]

Here, **for the sake of your name** marks the purpose for covering over their sins. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that people will honor your name]
Here, **name** represents God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for the sake of your reputation]

10.note: Asaph is using the question form to argue that God should act so that the nations will not mock him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not let the nations say that their God cannot help them!]

The nations would be using the question form to mock Israel rather than to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Their God cannot help them!]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [Why should the nations ask where their God is]
The pronoun **their** refers to the people of Israel, spoken from the perspective of the nations. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is the God of Israel]

10.q: יִוָּדַ֣ע ב⁠גיים לְ⁠עֵינֵ֑י⁠נוּ נִ֝קְמַ֗ת דַּֽם־עֲבָדֶ֥י⁠ךָ הַ⁠שָּׁפֽוּךְ
10.note: The expression **be known among the nations** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let the nations see you carry out vengeance for killing your servants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you avenge]

The psalmist is speaking as if someone had actually **poured out** the **blood** of Yahweh’s **servants** from a vessel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the shedding of the blood of your servants]

Here, **the poured-out blood** represents the violent killing of God’s servants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the killing of your servants]

The expression **the poured-out blood** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the blood that the nations have shed]
Here, **eyes** represents sight and perception. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [so that we can see it]

11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **groaning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the prisoners groan]
Here, **face** represents God’s presence and attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your great arm]
Here, **arm** represents God’s power and strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your power]

Asaph is using **sons of death** as a common expression to mean “those who are destined to die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who are condemned to die]

12.note: Asaph says **sevenfold** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [many times over]

Asaph is using **into their bosom** as a common expression to mean “directly and personally to them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [directly upon them]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could put the object **their reproach with which they have reproached you** before the other information in the sentence, so that the reader understands right away what is to be returned. Alternate translation: [And return their reproach with which they have reproached you, Lord, to our neighbors sevenfold, into their bosom]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the insults they have spoken]

13.note: Asaph places **And we** at the beginning of this verse to mark a shift from petition to a vow of praise. If it would be more natural in your language, you could indicate this transition in another way. Alternate translation: [Then we]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were a **flock** of sheep that God tends in his **pasture**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones you tend and care for]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **flock** that is located in God’s **pasture**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the flock that feeds in your pasture]
This concluding vow of praise signals the end of the psalm. Use the natural form in your language for signaling that a song or poem is ending. Alternate translation: [will always give thanks to you]
Asaph says **forever** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [always]

Asaph says **to generation and generation** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [in every generation that follows]

Asaph is using a poetic device found in the original language by repeating the word **generation** to express the idea of an unending succession. This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate this kind of poetic repetition, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [from one generation to the next]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how praiseworthy you are]
